summary:
TerraTwin is an independent planetary terrain-analogue discovery platform that explores how Earth's landscapes compare with the surfaces of Mars and the Moon. By combining geospatial analysis, machine learning, and deep learning-based terrain representation, TerraTwin aims to identify morphologically similar locations, compare terrain characteristics across different worlds, and create interactive 3D Terrain Twins. It also provides evidence-based insights into how suitable Earth locations may be for planetary exploration experiments, while highlighting data limitations and uncertainty.


Video - https://youtu.be/4JtGTbnIA9E

One Earth. Different Worlds. Shared Terrain Patterns.
details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

TerraTwin is an independent planetary terrain-analogue discovery platform designed to identify locations on Earth that share morphological similarities with selected regions of Mars and the Moon. It aims to help planetary scientists and mission planners identify useful Earth-based environments for testing exploration technologies and studying terrain-related challenges before deploying them on other planetary bodies.

The platform processes Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) from Earth and planetary datasets. Its ScaleBridge component harmonizes coordinate reference systems, spatial coverage, resolution, and measurement characteristics so that comparisons are scientifically meaningful. Its Terrain Analytics engine extracts features such as slope, local relief, surface roughness, curvature, Topographic Position Index, and landform morphology.

TerraTwin incorporates a machine learning and deep learning pipeline to learn terrain representations from DEM patches. A self-supervised CNN-based encoder is being developed to generate terrain embeddings, allowing the system to retrieve morphologically similar regions beyond simple feature-by-feature comparisons. Learned similarity is evaluated separately from physically interpretable terrain measurements to maintain transparency.

The platform then generates an interactive 3D Terrain Twin from the selected elevation data and produces an Analogue Evidence Passport containing candidate locations, terrain comparisons, data provenance, model information, uncertainty, and experiment-transferability considerations.

What benefits does it provide?

  • Helps researchers discover potential Earth-based analogues for planetary terrain.
  • Reduces the manual effort involved in screening large geographic regions.
  • Combines measurable terrain characteristics with learned deep-learning representations.
  • Provides interactive 3D terrain visualization for easier interpretation.
  • Makes comparisons explainable through documented measurements, data sources, and model limitations.
  • Helps distinguish terrain properties that can be tested on Earth from those requiring planetary conditions.

What is the intended impact?

TerraTwin aims to support more informed and accessible planetary exploration research. By connecting Earth observation data with planetary topography and AI-based terrain understanding, it can help researchers identify candidate field-testing environments for rover mobility, autonomous navigation, and terrain exploration.

Its long-term impact is to create a reusable framework for comparing landscapes across planetary bodies, supporting mission preparation, scientific investigation, and the development of exploration technologies.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project is being developed using:

  • Python: Core geospatial processing, data preparation, scientific computation, and backend services.
  • PyTorch: Development and training of deep-learning terrain representation models.
  • NumPy and SciPy: Numerical and scientific computation.
  • GDAL and Rasterio: DEM ingestion and raster processing.
  • GeoPandas, Shapely, and PyProj: Geospatial operations and coordinate transformations.
  • FastAPI: Backend API development.
  • PostgreSQL and PostGIS: Storage and querying of geospatial information.
  • TypeScript and Next.js: Frontend application development.
  • MapLibre GL JS: Interactive geographic visualization.
  • Three.js: Interactive 3D terrain visualization.
  • Docker: Reproducible development and deployment environments.

NASA planetary and Earth-observation datasets, including MOLA and SRTM products, are among the intended data sources. The specific products and versions used are recorded for provenance and reproducibility.

How is the project creative and innovative?

TerraTwin goes beyond conventional terrain visualization by combining geospatial science, machine learning, and 3D terrain reconstruction within a single discovery workflow. Rather than relying exclusively on manually selected terrain measurements, its deep-learning pipeline aims to learn morphological representations from elevation data and retrieve similar terrain patterns across different planetary bodies.

Its distinctive contribution is the combination of two complementary forms of evidence: interpretable physical terrain measurements and learned terrain representations. The system also connects analogue discovery with experiment-transferability assessment, helping users understand not only which locations look similar but also which terrain properties may be useful for testing planetary exploration technologies.

What factors did we consider?

Scientific reliability, dataset quality, differences in spatial resolution, coordinate systems, vertical references, missing observations, geographic coverage, model generalization, and computational requirements were central design considerations.

We also considered the limitations of Earth-based analogues. Similar terrain geometry does not guarantee identical soil composition, gravity, atmospheric conditions, radiation exposure, or mechanical behavior. TerraTwin therefore aims to communicate uncertainty and distinguish directly comparable terrain properties from conditions that require additional evidence or cannot be reproduced on Earth.

Our guiding principle is that AI-generated similarity should support scientific investigation, not replace physical evidence or scientific validation.
